parts: Your gas meter counts gas one gulp at a time.
Nothing flashes. Nobody presses a button. Yet every bill starts from those little numbers.
So how does a gas meter know how much gas you used?
According to Wikipedia, the most common type in homes is the diaphragm meter, also called a bellows meter.
Other designs exist, such as rotary meters, for higher volumes, and ultrasonic ones, mostly in high-flow pipeline stations.
Inside a home meter, movable diaphragms form two or more chambers. Valves steer the gas so the chambers take turns filling and emptying, which keeps the flow nearly continuous.
Our comparison: it is like a seesaw that never rests. One chamber fills while the other empties.
Levers and cranks turn that back-and-forth motion into a spinning shaft.
The shaft drives a counter, much like the odometer in a car.
Gas comes in, a chamber fills, the valves switch, and the counter moves a tiny step.
Here is our reading. The meter does not time the gas. It counts how many times its chambers filled.
What the meter itself counts is volume, in cubic metres or in cubic feet, depending on the meter.
Like a car odometer, it is a running total. The bill uses the difference between two readings.
That is one reason meters get read. Without a recent reading, a supplier may send an estimated bill.
One supplier says an estimate can leave you paying too much or too little.
Smart meters can send readings automatically. But another supplier says that if a smart meter stops reporting, bills can be estimated until readings arrive.
Here is a twist. In places like Belgium and the UK, you are billed for energy, not for volume.
Wikipedia says volume ignores the quality of the gas and the heat it gives when burned.
So the company converts, using the gas's calorific value. That is the heat released when it burns. Wikipedia says gas quality is measured and adjusted each billing cycle.
A Belgian guide says that value varies with the gas's origin and composition, so the same volume can carry different energy.
It gives about eleven and a half kilowatt-hours per cubic metre as typical in Brussels.
Wikipedia adds that temperature and pressure change a gas volume, so corrections are applied, in the meter or in the billing system.
Then the supplier multiplies the energy by the unit price in your contract, plus other charges.
So the numbers on your meter are not your bill. They are a running total of gas.
Here is our reading. A gas meter is a counter that turns something invisible into something you can pay for.
Gas reaches your home through a pipe. A phone call used to reach it through a wire. Today, you never think about either.
How did a phone call find its way before computers?
